title: introducing dettato — kobimusic
excerpt: a SOTA audio to midi model that significantly beats MuScriptor 1.3B and scores a bit higher than Mirelo's closed source model, at 20m parameters, trained on no copyrighted recordings.
content_html:
16 November 2026

we're introducing Dettato, a SOTA audio to MIDI transcription model that significantly beats MuScriptor 1.3B - the next best open model - and scores a bit higher than mirelo's closed source model 'Mirelo A2M v1.1 Pro' on their published benchmarks. all at just 20m parameters - roughly 65x smaller than muscriptor. Additionally, in training the model, we trained on absolutely no copyrighted recordings. the model is open source and you can use its outputs for commercial purposes.

disclaimer with the benchmarks: it's difficult to gauge the true accuracy of the model for your use-case without trying it yourself. one thing my model performs poor on for instance, is splitting instruments correctly. In addition, this just spits out performance MIDI with a beat aligned. If you're looking for something that you can actually play(e.g sheet music), i'd reccommend songscription or klangio - both are excellent tools by great companies that push the envelope of what's possible in this field forward.

0:00 / 0:00

sousa, the stars and stripes forever: “the president's own” united states marine band, from the complete marches of john philip sousa, vol. 3. a us government recording, public domain. download the MIDI

the driving goal of kobimusic: to help musicians, not replace them. a part of that goal means following copyright law. we trained dettato on a mix of synthetic instrument recordings and CC solo instruments mixed in using the URMP dataset. the rest of the instruments morph together ~20 soundfonts, using the 'soundfont babies' technique i published. no copyrighted recordings were used.

I began working on dettato about 10 months ago, but scrapped what I had in about April. The reason why was that I treated AMT as a data problem - but in reality, the bottleneck is architecture. There are a lot of parellels that you can draw for OMR (first model i made) and AMT. both traditionally were tackled early on using algorithms. later, in both fields they plugged in giant LLM components. These models would naturally become overfit to synthetic data, since globally the problems of AMT and OMR become different than if you treat it locally. But, for both you can reframe it as a local problem. For OMR, using a detector model. For AMT, a pitch-lane model.

overall, i hope both open and closed weight music retrieval companies can learn from this. The constraint of not using copyrighted recordings doesn't hold you back, but actually encourages innovation, and it's likely you'll end up with a better model in the end.
